decided.text: Explicit flags beat the inference — --no-token, then --token X, then --token, then the bind check. A rule that could not be overridden would strand anyone on a trusted LAN

flags.text: The check cannot catch a SYNTAX error — imports resolve before it runs. If a future edit uses newer syntax, old Node dies before line 28 and this is useless

decided.text: Test servers bind 127.0.0.1 rather than threading tokens through every curl — they never needed the LAN, and it also stops the suite triggering a firewall prompt on a stranger's first run
Pinned the rule with 13 new checks instead of just unbreaking the old ones; the restart-keeps-the-token case is the one that matters, since a rotating token would break the phone link it protects

questions.title: What does "public" mean here — a repo people clone, or a plugin they install?
questions.spoken: First thing: how do you picture someone actually getting this? Today the readme says clone it into your skills folder. There's also the Claude Code plugin marketplace, where installing is one command and updates arrive on their own. Which of those is the front door?
questions.context:
The README today says:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/MusabIlhan/grill-board.git ~/.claude/skills/grill-board
```

That works, and it is what `/grill-me` does too. But it makes **you** the update mechanism: nobody who cloned in August finds out that the Start-building button exists.

| | clone into `~/.claude/skills` | plugin marketplace | npm package |
|---|---|---|---|
| install | one `git clone` | `/plugin install` | `npx grill-board` |
| updates | they `git pull`, if they remember | handled | `npx` is always latest |
| needs | nothing | a `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` + repo layout | a publish pipeline, a name nobody owns |
| discoverable | only if you link it | listed | npm search |
| the skill itself | already correct | paths inside SKILL.md hardcode `~/.claude/skills/grill-board` — those break | same problem, worse |

The path question is the sharp edge: every command in SKILL.md is written as `node ~/.claude/skills/grill-board/board.mjs`. Under a plugin that directory is `~/.claude/plugins/…/grill-board`, so the skill has to resolve its own location instead of hardcoding it. That is a real change, not a docs edit.
questions.recommendation: Clone, and say so plainly — same front door as /grill-me, zero new machinery, and the thing you are shipping is a skill people read before they trust. A marketplace entry is the right second move once someone other than you has run it.

options.label: Clone into ~/.claude/skills, like grill-me
options.detail: Ships today. No update path — you'd be pushing tags and hoping people pull.

options.label: Claude Code plugin marketplace
options.detail: Real installs and real updates. Costs: repo restructure, self-locating paths in SKILL.md, and a manifest to keep right.

options.label: Both — clone now, plugin as v2
options.detail: Honest, but the second half is the one that never happens unless you date it.

questions.title: What are you actually signing up for once strangers have it?
questions.spoken: Second: what do you owe people afterwards? There's a version where this is a thing you built and put up, take it or leave it. And a version where you answer issues and take pull requests. Those need different files in the repo, and it's much easier to say which one you are up front than to walk it back later.
questions.context:
This decides several files at once, so it is worth settling before the polish work rather than after.

| | "here it is" | maintained |
|---|---|---|
| LICENCE | still needed — **no licence means nobody may legally use it** | same |
| README tone | "I built this for me" | "contributions welcome" |
| issues | off, or a note saying they go unanswered | on, with a template |
| PRs | a line saying you probably won't merge them | CONTRIBUTING.md, a test command that works on someone else's machine |
| breaking changes | free | you owe a CHANGELOG |
| the state file format | free to change | people have boards in flight |

The repo is **private with no licence today**. That one is not optional in any version — "no licence" is the default-deny state, so a public repo with no LICENCE file is one nobody may legally copy, and putting it off means the first ten people who find it can't use it.
questions.recommendation: "Here it is", MIT, issues on but expectations set in the README. It costs one file and one paragraph, and it does not commit your evenings to a tool you built for yourself.

options.label: "Here it is" — MIT, no promises
options.detail: One LICENCE file, one honest README line. You can upgrade later; you cannot downgrade.

options.label: Properly maintained
options.detail: CONTRIBUTING, issue templates, a CHANGELOG, and a test suite that passes on a machine that is not yours.

options.label: Archive it read-only
options.detail: Public to read, issues and PRs off. Least work, and it says 'do not build on this'.

questions.title: What is the bar for v1 — does it work, or does it land?
questions.spoken: Third, and this one shapes everything else: what has to be true before you press publish? There's a low bar — a stranger clones it and it works on their machine. And a high one — someone sees the page and understands in thirty seconds why they'd want it. They need completely different work, and one of them is mostly writing rather than code.
questions.context:
Same repo, two very different piles of work.

**"It works"** — the failure modes a stranger hits that you never will:
- Node version floor (you are on whatever your Mac has; the README says 18+ — is that tested?)
- The board writes to `~/.claude/grill-board/…`, which assumes a `~/.claude` exists
- `test-build.sh` binds real ports from 7896 and shells out to `curl`; on a machine with a busy port or no curl it fails and looks like the tool is broken
- Ports 7800+ and the `0.0.0.0` bind — a corporate laptop firewall prompt on first run is a bad first impression
- Nothing has ever run on Linux or Windows/WSL

**"It lands"** — the repo as an argument:
- The README already reads well, but there is **not a single screenshot or GIF** of the actual board. A tool whose whole pitch is a page you look at, shown only as ASCII art.
- No demo anyone can try without installing
- `/grill-me` gets to say "it's like being interviewed"; grill-board has to explain a board, a build panel, a checklist and a review in one screen of text

They are not mutually exclusive — but they compete for the next day of work, and whichever you name is where it goes.
questions.recommendation: "It lands." A stranger who cannot tell what this is never gets far enough to hit a portability bug — and the one thing missing is the cheapest to fix: a picture of the board.

options.label: It lands — the page has to sell it
options.detail: Screenshots or a GIF of a real board, a tightened README opening. Mostly writing and a screen recording.

options.label: It works — portability first
options.detail: Node floor, a clean-machine run, Linux, no-curl fallback in the tests. Invisible if nobody clones it.

options.label: Both, and it slips a week
options.detail: The honest answer if you want it to survive contact. Say so and I will plan it as two phases.

questions.title: You said it has to land. So what does a stranger actually SEE?
questions.spoken: You picked "it lands", so here's the sharpest version of that. Right now there is not one picture of the board anywhere in the readme — a tool whose whole pitch is a page you look at, shown only as ascii art. Four ways to fix that, and they cost very different amounts. Do you want static screenshots, an animated gif of a real grill, or a live demo page people can click?
questions.context:
The README is 326 lines and genuinely well written, and it contains **zero images**. Every illustration is ASCII:

```
Building what you decided                          2/4
  ✓  Split retryable vs terminal in classifyError   q1 q3
```

That is charming in a terminal README and it is *not* what the thing looks like. The board has eight palettes, a card layout, a word-level diff, a build panel and a checklist — and a reader has to take all of it on faith.

| | what it costs | what it proves |
|---|---|---|
| **Static screenshots** (3–4 PNGs) | ~30 min: run a real grill, screenshot card / build panel / diff / checklist | what it looks like |
| **Animated GIF** | ~1–2 h: script a run, record, trim, keep it under GitHub's 10 MB inline limit | that it is *live* — cards appearing while you answer is the whole idea and a still cannot show it |
| **Live demo on GitHub Pages** | unknown, see below | that it is real, and it is clickable from the README |
| **asciinema of the CLI side** | ~30 min | the wrong half — nobody cares what the CLI prints |

On the live demo: `board.html` is a single self-contained file, but it is **not** static-ready. It polls `GET /api/state` every 400–2500 ms and POSTs to `/api/answer`, `/api/ask`, `/api/message`, `/api/prefs`, `/api/start`. A Pages demo needs those six intercepted against a canned state — a small shim, but I have not written or measured it, so treat "cheap" as unverified.

The honest ranking is: **a GIF is the one that carries the idea**, because "you are never blocked" is a claim about *time*, and a still image cannot make it.
questions.recommendation: GIF at the top, then two or three stills further down for the build panel and the diff. Skip the live demo for v1 — it is the only option here with an unknown number attached, and it is trying to prove something the GIF already proves.

options.label: One GIF up top + a few stills below
options.detail: Shows the live-ness, which is the actual claim. Half a day, mostly recording and trimming.

options.label: Stills only
options.detail: Half an hour, and the README stops lying by omission. Does not show that cards arrive while you answer.

options.label: Live clickable demo on GitHub Pages
options.detail: Strongest proof, unknown cost, and a second copy of board.html to keep in sync.

options.label: Ship with no images
options.detail: It reads well enough to survive. I think this is wrong for a tool that is literally a screen.

questions.title: The board binds to 0.0.0.0 with no password. Is that OK to hand a stranger?
questions.spoken: Here's the one I'd want you to look at hardest before it goes public. By default the board listens on every network interface, and by default there's no token — so anyone on the same wifi can read your plan and, worse, answer your questions. On your home network that's the feature that lets you answer from your phone. On café wifi handed to someone who never read that line, it's a leak.
questions.context:
```js
// board.mjs:1264
const host = args.host || '0.0.0.0';
```

and `--token` is **opt-in**. So the default run is: readable *and writable* by anything that can reach port 7800+.

The README does say so — but in the voice-mode section, ~250 lines down:

> **`--token` is not optional once the board leaves your machine.**

That is a warning for the person who has read the whole page. The person who runs `/grill-board` on day one has read the first screen.

What is actually at stake: the state file holds the plan, the code in the cards, the diffs of changes, and every answer. Writable means someone else can answer a card, which the session then acts on — that is not just a privacy leak, it is an **injection path into what gets built**.

| | keep `0.0.0.0`, no token | `127.0.0.1` default, `--lan` opts in | `0.0.0.0` but auto-mint a token |
|---|---|---|---|
| phone answering | works out of the box | one extra flag, discovered by reading | works, URL carries `?t=…` |
| café wifi | exposed | safe | readable only with the URL |
| breaks today's behaviour | no | yes — the LAN URL stops working unless asked for | no |
| README has to explain | the risk | the flag | nothing |

The third one is interesting: the URL file already prints a LAN address, and it could simply print it *with the token in it*. Cost is roughly "default `--token` on when host is not loopback".
questions.recommendation: Auto-mint a token whenever the bind is not loopback. It keeps the phone feature working with no new flag to learn, it makes the insecure-by-default state impossible to reach by accident, and the URL file already exists to carry it.

options.label: Auto-token whenever it binds beyond loopback
options.detail: Phone still works, URL carries ?t=. Nothing to learn, nothing to break.

options.label: Default to 127.0.0.1, --lan to open it
options.detail: Safest and simplest to explain. Breaks the phone flow for anyone who does not read.

options.label: Leave it, move the warning to the top of the README
options.detail: Zero code. Relies on strangers reading a warning, which is the assumption that fails.

options.label: Auto-token AND loopback default
options.detail: Belt and braces. Two behaviour changes at once for a tool nobody has complained about yet.

questions.title: SKILL.md is 685 lines. Every invocation pays for it. Does it get split?
questions.spoken: Last one for now, and it's about a cost that's invisible to you but not to the people who install it. Grill-me is ten lines. Grill-board's instructions are six hundred and eighty five, about forty kilobytes, and Claude loads the whole thing every single time the skill runs — including the parts about splitting a build across several agents, which most runs never touch. Is that fine, or does it need to be a short core with the rest loaded on demand?
questions.context:
Measured just now:

| | lines | bytes |
|---|---|---|
| `grill-me/SKILL.md` | 10 | 635 |
| `grill-board/SKILL.md` | **685** | **39,614** |

About 10k tokens on **every** invocation, before a single question is written. Roughly a third of it is the multi-agent section, which a solo grill never uses, and the change-entry and card-writing examples, which only matter past the drain.

This is not only about cost. A long skill file is also a **quality** question in both directions: more instruction means more of it is followed, and also more of it competes for attention. You have tuned this one against your own runs; you genuinely do not know how it behaves for someone whose first grill is a Django app.

The split, if you did one, is natural — SKILL.md keeps the loop and the card rules, and points to files loaded only when reached:

```
SKILL.md          the loop, card writing, the rules      (~250 lines)
BUILDING.md       plan → start → build → test → review   (~200)
FANNING-OUT.md    claim, --decided, per-agent cursors    (~150)
```

The cost is real: a skill that references sibling files depends on Claude actually going and reading them at the right moment, and **that is exactly the failure this tool's own build phase exists to prevent** — a step that gets skipped is invisible until the output is wrong.
questions.recommendation: Leave it whole for v1. It is long because it is doing something long, splitting it introduces a new way to fail silently, and 10k tokens is not what will stop anyone using this. Revisit if someone reports the build phase going off the rails.

options.label: Leave it whole
options.detail: Zero risk, zero work. Costs ~10k tokens a run, which nobody has complained about.

options.label: Split into core + two loaded-on-demand files
options.detail: Cheaper runs and a more readable skill. Adds a silent failure mode: the file that never gets read.

options.label: Trim it instead — cut 200 lines of prose
options.detail: Keeps one file. Every line you cut is a rule you decided you did not need, which is a real edit, not a formatting pass.

questions.title: On the demo — can they answer a card, or only look at one?
questions.spoken: You picked the live demo, so here's the fork that decides how much work it is. A demo where you can only look is basically a screenshot with extra steps. A demo where you can actually answer a card and watch the next one appear is the entire pitch, working, in someone's browser before they install anything. The second one means faking six endpoints against a state that lives in the page.
questions.context:
The page is one self-contained file, but it talks to a server on six routes:

```
GET  /api/state     polled every 400–2500ms — this is how cards appear
POST /api/answer    /api/ask  /api/message  /api/prefs  /api/start
```

A static host has none of those. So the demo needs a shim that answers all six from memory. What differs is how much it has to fake.

| | read-only | answerable | scripted playback |
|---|---|---|---|
| what it shows | the layout | **the loop** — answer, next card appears | the loop, on rails |
| shim work | stub `GET /api/state`, hide the buttons | all six, plus a tiny fake session that adds cards on a timer after an answer | all six, plus a timeline |
| can they break it | no | yes — they will answer everything and hit the end | no |
| honest? | yes | yes, if the follow-ups are pre-written and it says so | **only if labelled** — a fake Claude that always says the same thing is a demo, not a lie, but it has to look like one |
| my guess at cost | ~1 h | ~3–4 h | ~4–5 h |

The trap in all three is the same and it is worth naming now: **a forked copy of `board.html` rots.** You have already been bitten by a running server serving old code, and the fix there was a version handshake. A demo copy is that failure with no warning attached — the README's demo silently becomes a picture of last month's board.

The way out is to not fork it: build the demo as `board.html` **plus** a small `demo.js` that installs a `fetch` interceptor before the page's first poll, and have CI (or the test script) fail if the two files drift. Then there is one page, and the demo is a wrapper.
questions.recommendation: Answerable, built as a fetch shim over the real board.html — not a fork. Read-only is a screenshot you paid three hours for, and playback is more work than answerable for less proof.

options.label: Answerable, shim over the real board.html
options.detail: They answer a card and the follow-up lands. One page, no fork, ~3–4h.

options.label: Read-only snapshot
options.detail: ~1h and it does render the real thing. Proves layout, not the loop — which is what you said had to land.

options.label: Scripted playback, hands off
options.detail: Cards and answers appear on a timeline. Most control over what they see, most work, and they cannot touch it.

options.label: Answerable now, playback later if it isn't landing
options.detail: Fine, as long as 'later' means you would actually measure whether it lands.

questions.title: grill-me's whole README is 200 words. Yours is 326 lines. Which is right?
questions.spoken: I read grill-me's github page. Title, one paragraph, install, done — under two hundred words, no pictures, no badges. It works because the skill itself is ten lines: you can read the entire thing in a minute. Yours is a five and a half thousand line project and the readme is three hundred and twenty six lines. That's not automatically wrong, but it does mean the first screen is doing a different job, and I want to know which job you think it's doing.
questions.context:
Measured, both:

| | grill-me | grill-board |
|---|---|---|
| README | ~200 words, 4 sections | 326 lines, ~15 KB, 8 sections |
| the skill | 10 lines | 685 lines |
| the code | none | 4,300 lines |
| images | none | none |

grill-me's page can be short because there is nothing behind it to explain. Yours has a build phase, a checklist, a review loop, multi-agent claiming, an MCP voice server and a gateway — and the README currently explains **all** of them, in order, well.

The question is who the page is for. Right now it reads as **documentation for someone who has decided**, and the pitch — the part that makes a stranger decide — is the first 30 lines. Everything after "Answering" is reference.

| | leave it | pitch on top, reference in `docs/` | cut it to grill-me length |
|---|---|---|---|
| a stranger scrolling | reads 3 screens before the payoff | sees the whole argument in one | sees a claim with nothing behind it |
| someone who installed it | everything is where they left it | one extra click | has to read SKILL.md |
| work | none | ~1 h of moving, no rewriting | a rewrite, and you lose the good parts |
| what it costs you | the good writing is buried past the fold | a `docs/` folder to keep current | the multi-agent and voice sections stop being discoverable |

Note what is *not* in question: the writing is good. This is about order, not quality.
questions.recommendation: Pitch on top, reference below or in docs/. The first screen becomes GIF-or-demo, the three-line what-it-is, and install — and everything you have already written survives one scroll further down.

options.label: Pitch on top, reference moves down or into docs/
options.detail: Keeps every word you wrote; changes what the first screen is for. ~1h of moving.

options.label: Leave it — it reads well as one page
options.detail: True. The cost is that the demo, the install and the argument are separated by two screens of scrolling.

options.label: Cut hard to grill-me length, link out for the rest
options.detail: Matches the reference you named. You lose the thing that makes this page persuasive, which is the detail.

questions.title: Your first paragraph compares it to /grill-me. There is no official /grill-me.
questions.spoken: Something I found while looking up grill-me, and it changes your opening. There isn't one grill-me. I found at least eight separate github repos and gists all called some version of it, plus directory listings — none of them official, none canonical. So your second sentence, the one that carries the whole pitch, compares your tool to something the reader may never have heard of and can't reliably go and look up. The question is whether the pitch should stand on its own instead.
questions.context:
The README's second paragraph, which is where a stranger decides:

> `/grill-me` asks one question, then waits. You answer, it thinks, you wait again.
> `grill-board` posts questions to a page you keep open…

That is a **great** sentence for someone who has used grill-me. Searching for it turns up robmitt/grill-me-skill, stevegsax/grill-me, Jekudy/grillme-skill, at least four collection repos with their own copy, a gist, and two directory sites. No official one. The most-linked README is under 200 words and its skill is 10 lines.

So the comparison does three things at once, and only one of them is good:

- ✅ instantly clear **to the ~5% who know it**
- ❌ jargon to everyone else, in the sentence that decides whether they keep reading
- ❌ frames a 5,500-line tool as "like that small thing, but async" — which undersells it and invites "why is this not 10 lines too?"

The alternative is to lead with the problem, which needs no priors: *you are answering an agent's questions one at a time, blocked, in a chat log — and the questions are too small because a chat line is small.*

| | keep the comparison | lead with the problem | both — problem first, comparison as an aside |
|---|---|---|---|
| reader with no priors | lost for one paragraph | in immediately | in immediately |
| reader who knows grill-me | instant | one extra sentence | instant, one line down |
| sells the build/review half | no — it frames it as a Q&A tool | yes | yes |
questions.recommendation: Lead with the problem, keep the comparison as a one-line aside further down. The build-and-review half is more than half the tool, and the current opening does not mention it at all.

options.label: Lead with the problem; comparison becomes an aside
options.detail: Works with no priors, and lets the first screen say that it builds and reviews too.

options.label: Keep the comparison up top
options.detail: Sharpest sentence you have, for the readers who already get it. Costs you everyone else.

options.label: Drop grill-me entirely
options.detail: Cleanest positioning. Loses a genuinely useful shorthand and the credit for the idea.

questions.title: There is no troubleshooting section, and first-run failures are silent-ish
questions.spoken: Good news first: I read the code for portability and it's much better than I implied earlier. Five node builtins, no shelling out, nothing mac-only — it should just run on linux. Only the test script is bash-and-curl. So the risk isn't that it breaks, it's what happens in the handful of cases where it does, because right now the readme has eight sections and none of them is 'it didn't work'.
questions.context:
What I verified in `board.mjs`:

- imports only `node:http`, `node:fs`, `node:path`, `node:url`, `node:os` — no dependencies, **no `execSync`, no `lsof`, no `pbcopy`**, nothing mac-only
- state directories are `mkdirSync(..., { recursive: true })`, so a missing `~/.claude` is not a failure
- ports auto-select across 7800–7859, and it dies with a clear message past that

So it is portable. What is left is the small set of first-run failures a stranger *will* hit, none of which the README addresses:

| | what they see | what is actually wrong |
|---|---|---|
| Node too old | a syntax error in a 2,100-line file | README says 18+; **nothing enforces or tests it** — no `engines`, no runtime check |
| all 60 ports busy | `no free port in 7800-7859` | fine, actually — this one is good |
| board opens, stays empty | a page saying "No questions yet" | usually correct; sometimes the session died |
| corporate firewall prompt | macOS/Windows asks to allow incoming connections | the `0.0.0.0` bind — related to q5 |
| they edit board.mjs while a board runs | writes accepted, page never updates | the version handshake catches it — for **you**; a stranger sees a dead board |

questions.title: Auto-token by bind address misses the gateway — the one thing meant to be public
questions.spoken: You picked auto-token whenever it binds beyond loopback, and I went to check it didn't break the voice setup. Good news there — it doesn't, the gateway is completely independent. But checking turned up a hole in the rule itself. The gateway binds to loopback, and then you tunnel it to the open internet with cloudflared. The process can't see the tunnel. So the one surface you deliberately put on the public internet is the exact one a bind-address rule leaves unprotected.
questions.context:
First, the thing I checked, so you can stop worrying about it: **the gateway does not proxy through `serve`.** It calls `makeHandler(getCurrent)` and reads the current board's state file directly, with its own `prefs.gatewayToken`. Auto-minting a token on `serve` cannot break a registered connector.

Now the hole:

```js
// cmdGateway, board.mjs:2056
const host = args.host || '127.0.0.1';   // loopback…
```

…and then your own README says to do this:

```bash
cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:7799   # or: ngrok http 7799
```

The bind is loopback. The reachability is *the entire internet*. A rule keyed on the bind address sees a safe-looking `127.0.0.1` and mints nothing.

| | today | q5's rule as stated | gateway always tokened |
|---|---|---|---|
| `serve` on your Mac | open on LAN, no token | tokened ✅ | tokened ✅ |
| `gateway` + cloudflared | **open to the internet, no token** | **still open** ❌ | tokened ✅ |
| voice setup flow | `--token` documented, opt-in | unchanged | one less flag to remember |

And what is behind that URL is not read-only: `answer`, `ask_better` and `use_board` are all writable over `/mcp`. An untokened tunnel is a stranger answering your cards.

The README does warn — *"`--token` is not optional once the board leaves your machine"* — but that is the same bet q5 just declined to keep making.

The fix is small: the gateway exists **only** to be reached remotely, so it should mint a token unconditionally rather than asking the bind address a question it cannot answer.
questions.recommendation: Gateway always mints a token, no flag needed, with `--no-token` as the deliberate way out. It is the one command in this tool whose whole purpose is remote access — there is no version of it where a token is optional.

options.label: Gateway always tokens; --no-token to opt out
options.detail: Matches what the gateway is for. One less flag in the setup, and the insecure state needs typing.

options.label: Keep the bind rule everywhere, consistent
options.detail: One rule to explain. Leaves the tunnel case exactly as exposed as it is today.

options.label: Gateway refuses to start without --token
options.detail: Loudest, and impossible to get wrong. Breaks anyone's existing gateway command on upgrade.

questions.title: You're splitting SKILL.md. How does the second file actually get read?
questions.spoken: You went for the split, so the thing to settle is the failure mode I flagged — a file that never gets read. It's a real one and it's silent: Claude follows the short core, reaches the build phase, and just... carries on from memory instead of opening the file with the rules in it. Nothing errors. The board still fills up. It's only wrong in ways you'd notice a day later.
questions.context:
The split you picked, roughly:

```
SKILL.md          the loop, card writing, the rules      (~250 lines)
BUILDING.md       plan → start → build → test → review   (~200)
FANNING-OUT.md    claim, --decided, per-agent cursors    (~150)
```

Why this is not paranoia: the build phase is precisely where the instructions are **counter-intuitive and easy to skip**. Post the plan before reading a file. Wait for the button; never press it yourself. Log a change in the same breath as marking the step. Author the checklist before the review. Every one of those is a rule that *feels* skippable in the moment, and every one of them is in the file that might not get opened.

Four ways to make it stick, in increasing order of "actually works":

| | how it works | fails when |
|---|---|---|
| **Pointer in SKILL.md** | "When the board drains → read BUILDING.md" | the model is mid-flow and confident; a pointer is an instruction like any other |
| **Keep the traps, move the examples** | correctness stays in the core; the sub-file holds JSON samples and prose | nothing breaks — you just do not save many tokens, since the traps *are* most of the length |
| **The CLI says it on the wake** | `[drained]` already prints. Make it print `→ read BUILDING.md before you plan`. The session acts on wake lines all day | it does not — this rides machinery that already drives behaviour |
| **Both of the last two** | traps stay, examples move, and the wake points at the file anyway | belt and braces |

That third one is the interesting one and it is nearly free: `describe()` already formats every event, and `[drained]` is the exact moment the build phase begins. Same for `[start]` → the checklist rules. The pointer arrives **when it is needed** rather than 250 lines earlier, which is the whole idea behind splitting in the first place.

The honest counter: it couples the skill's file layout to strings inside `board.mjs`, so renaming a file silently breaks the pointer. That is a `test-build.sh` check — assert every filename the CLI names exists on disk.
questions.recommendation: Wake-line pointers plus keeping the traps in the core. The pointer arrives at the moment of need instead of being remembered from earlier, and a filename check in the test suite closes the one new way it can rot.

options.detail: The reminder lands when the phase starts, and correctness never depended on the second file being opened. One new test.

There's about a full day of work on this board and one item on it can silently break the skill. So the question isn't whether to post today. It's which of these ships before you do.

Everything settled so far, costed, in the order it would have to happen:

| | from | cost | HN-critical? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **LICENCE (MIT)** | q2 | 5 min | **yes** — no licence is a guaranteed top comment, and it is the one that makes the repo unusable |
| **Auto-token past loopback** | q5 | ~30 min + test | **yes** — HN is the exact audience that reads `0.0.0.0` and no auth and says so publicly |

That is roughly 7–10 hours, which is a day with nothing going wrong.

**The split is the item to move.** It is the only change on this list that touches how the skill *behaves*, it has no test that would catch it going wrong, and its entire payoff is token cost — which is invisible to every person who reads your HN post. Shipping a freshly-restructured 685-line instruction file on the morning of a launch is how the first stranger's grill goes sideways in a way you find out about in the comments.

Also worth saying plainly: **q2 was "here it is, no promises", and HN is the one venue where that gets tested hardest.** That combination is fine — plenty of good tools ship that way — but a README line saying it out loud, before the comments arrive, reads as a stance. The same line written afterwards reads as a retreat.

questions.title: serve mints a token whenever it binds past loopback
questions.spoken: The board now gives itself a password whenever it listens on the network, which is the default. Your phone still works — the link just carries the token now. On localhost only, it stays open, and there's a no-token flag if you want it open on a network you trust. I checked that restarting keeps the same token, so a link already open on a phone doesn't break.
questions.spokenDetail:
A board bound to `0.0.0.0` — which is still the default, so the phone still works — now comes up with a token, and every URL it prints carries `?t=`. Bound to `127.0.0.1` it stays open, because nothing but you can reach it.

The insecure-by-default state is no longer reachable by accident. It is still reachable **on purpose**: `--no-token` serves it open on a network you trust.

The rule is one expression, and the order matters — an explicit flag always beats the inference:

```js

  : args.token ? true                            // --token
  : !LOOPBACK.has(host);                         // the new bit
```

questions.title: The gateway always mints a token, because a tunnel is invisible to a bind check
questions.spoken: The gateway now always has a password. It binds to localhost and then you tunnel it to the internet — so checking the bind address tells you nothing, which is why it can't use the same rule the board uses. There's a no-token flag if you really want it open, and it warns you not to tunnel that. I checked a registered connector survives a restart.
questions.spokenDetail:
`gateway` now comes up tokened whether you ask or not, and `--no-token` is the only way to an open one — where it says so out loud: **`token NONE — --no-token was passed. Do not tunnel this.`**

This is the hole the bind rule from c2 could never close. The gateway binds `127.0.0.1`, which any address check reads as safe, and then your own README tells you to point `cloudflared` at it. The process cannot see the tunnel. So the one surface deliberately placed on the open internet was the one surface a bind rule left open.

What is behind that URL is not read-only: `answer`, `ask_better` and `use_board` are writable over `/mcp`. An untokened tunnel is a stranger answering your cards, and the session builds from the answers.

questions.spoken: Running it on an old Node used to throw an error from somewhere in the middle of two thousand lines, which reads as the tool being broken rather than the node being old. On an older Node the first thing a stranger saw was a runtime error partway through a 2,100-line file, which reads as *"this tool is broken"*, and that is not a bug report anyone files. It is a closed tab.

```
grill-board needs Node 18 or newer — this is Node 16.4.0.
  nvm install 18   (or brew install node / your package manager)
  Nothing else is required: no dependencies, nothing to build.
```

questions.title: The suite covers the token rule, and stops putting itself on the network
questions.spoken: Worth knowing: the token change broke thirty seven of the fifty seven tests, because they were all talking to boards over HTTP without one. That's the same thing that would happen to anyone who'd scripted against this. Fixed by pointing the test servers at localhost, and then adding thirteen new checks so the rule is actually pinned. Seventy checks now, all green.
questions.spokenDetail:
**The token change broke 37 of 57 checks.** Every test that talks to a board over HTTP was curling an untokened URL, and every one of them got a 401. That is worth saying plainly rather than burying: it is exactly what will happen to anyone who has scripted against a board, and it is the reason this step existed.

Two things fixed it, and the second is the point.

**Test servers now bind `127.0.0.1`.** They never needed the LAN, and there is a second benefit for a public repo: running the suite on a stranger's Mac or Windows box no longer triggers an *"allow incoming connections"* firewall prompt on first run.

**Then thirteen new checks, so the rule is pinned rather than worked around:**

```
== the board does not go on the network naked
  ok   binding past loopback mints one        ok   the token gets you in
  ok   and says why                           ok   so does a bearer header
  ok   an untokened read is refused           ok   and it survives a restart
  ok   loopback stays open                    ok   --no-token is a real way out
== the gateway is public by definition
  ok   it mints without being asked           ok   and refuses an untokened read
== an old Node is told, not crashed into
  ok   it exits nonzero   ok   and names the floor   ok   and how to fix it
```

The restart check is the one I care most about: it asserts a token survives `--adopt`, because a token that changed on restart would break the phone link it exists to protect.

questions.spoken: The demo works as a plain static page — I served it over http and it rendered sixteen cards and the eight build steps, with the read-only ribbon along the bottom. The important part is it isn't a copy of the board page: it's generated from the real one, and the test suite fails if anyone changes the page without regenerating. questions.spoken: The gif is done — eleven seconds, one megabyte, and it's at the top of the readme. It's not a screen recording: it replays this actual board, winding the cards back to unanswered and letting them forward a beat at a time, so everything in it was really written and really answered. questions.spokenDetail:
**`docs/grill-board.gif` — 16 frames, 11 seconds, 1.0 MB**, well inside GitHub's inline limit. It is now the first thing on the page, above the ASCII diagram, with the demo linked underneath it.

It is not a screen recording. `reel.mjs` **replays this actual board**: it winds the cards back to unanswered, then lets them forward one beat at a time — three cards, you answer one, three more appear, the board drains, the plan goes up and sits there waiting for **Start building**, then the steps tick over. Every word in it was really written and really answered, which is what q13 asked for and what an invented board never manages.

The pipeline is three commands and no dependencies beyond what was already on the machine:

```bash
node demo/reel.mjs <state.json>     # 16 standalone HTML frames
# headless Chrome --screenshot over each
ffmpeg -framerate 1.4 ... palettegen/paletteuse
```

**Frames render through `build.mjs`'s `render()` — the same function the demo uses.** Two renderers would drift, and the one that drifted would be the one nobody looks at until it is already in a README. The ribbon is suppressed for frames, since *"nothing is saved"* is noise on a page nobody is clicking.

**And a real bug caught on the way past.** `.gitignore` had a blanket `state.json` — which silently swallowed `demo/state.json`. The demo would have been committed as a page with no board in it, and the first person to load it would have seen an empty board. `!demo/state.json` now exempts it, verified with `git check-ignore` and a dry-run `git add`.
